answer.sourceLine: Christensen made this prediction, and it is the line he is most often quoted on. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries a fuller wording and cites a blog post of 28 June 2007 — and that page no longer resolves. We could not read it, and we could not reach an archived copy from this network, so no primary source was read for this page. Two things we can show: the documented text is longer than the version in circulation, with a sentence dropped between the two quoted here, and the square brackets in it are editorial insertions by whoever quoted him, not words we can show Christensen said.

source.heading: What the documented version says

docMeta.dd: A 2007 interview, as relayed by the blog post Wikiquote cites
“Clayton Christensen’s Innovator’s Dilemma says iPhone will fail”, Jeremy’s Blog, 28 June 2007 — now offline
Condensed — one sentence is dropped between the two in circulation, and the tail is cut
Attributed — the remark is his; the exact wording we could not read in a primary source

source.excerpt: [T]he prediction of [my disruption] theory would be that Apple won’t succeed with the iPhone. They’ve launched an innovation that the existing players in the industry are heavily motivated to beat: It’s not [truly] disruptive. History speaks pretty loudly on that, that the probability of success is going to be limited.
trail: The fuller wording comes from Wikiquote’s Clayton M. Christensen page ↗, in its sourced 2000s section, where it is cited to a blog post titled “Clayton Christensen’s Innovator’s Dilemma says iPhone will fail”, dated 28 June 2007.

That citation is dead. The host does not resolve from here, and this container cannot reach the Internet Archive’s web capture either, so we could not read the page Wikiquote relies on. We are recording that rather than quietly citing a link we never opened.

The remark is widely described as coming from a Businessweek interview of June 2007. We could not verify that, so we do not assert it, and we give no issue date, interviewer or page for it anywhere on this page.

What is checkable is the shape of the drift: the two sentences people quote are not consecutive. A sentence about incumbents being “heavily motivated to beat” the iPhone sits between them, and it is the part that actually states the theory’s reasoning.
source.cutTag: Clayton Christensen, 2007, as documented at Wikiquote
source.excerptNote: This is the text as Wikiquote ↗ prints it. Bold marks what the circulating two-sentence version leaves out — a whole sentence in the middle and the clause that closes the thought. The square brackets are editorial insertions made by whoever quoted him — including the capital in “[T]he” — so even the documented wording is not a clean transcript.
source.rightsNote: A 2007 interview remark is firmly within copyright in the United States, which reaches works published before 1931 only. The sentences are reproduced here as a short excerpt for identification, verification and criticism. We do not name a rightsholder: we could not read the original publication, so we could not establish which one it is.

author.heading: About Clayton Christensen
author.metaLine: 1952–2020 · American business academic · Harvard Business School
author.bio: Clayton Magleby Christensen (1952–2020) was an American academic and business consultant who developed the theory of disruptive innovation, introduced in his 1997 book The Innovator’s Dilemma and since called the most influential business idea of the early 21st century. He was the Kim B. Clark Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School, and The Economist named him the most influential management thinker of his time.

misattribution.heading: Often mis-worded, and often shrunk
misattribution.intro: We found nobody disputing that Christensen said this. What happens to it is compression — each retelling a little shorter and a little more confident.

items.why: The documented text runs longer in both directions. Between “the iPhone” and “History speaks pretty loudly” sits the sentence that carries the actual argument — that Apple had launched something incumbents were heavily motivated to beat — and the closing clause, “that the probability of success is going to be limited”, is cut too. See Wikiquote’s entry ↗.

That is the headline of the very blog post Wikiquote cites — “Clayton Christensen’s Innovator’s Dilemma says iPhone will fail” — and it is a summariser’s phrase, not Christensen’s. He predicted limited probability of success against motivated incumbents, which is a narrower claim than the slogan it became.

misattribution.truthLine: Best available: Wikiquote’s sourced 2000s section ↗, citing a blog post of 28 June 2007 that is now offline. We could not read a primary source, and we stop at “attributed” for that reason.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Christensen introduced “disruption” in The Innovator’s Dilemma ↗ (1997), the book that described how large incumbents lose by listening to their best customers while cheaper, worse products improve underneath them. Wikipedia ↗ notes the idea has been called the most influential business idea of the early 21st century.

Which is what makes the iPhone call interesting rather than merely wrong. His theory distinguishes sustaining innovations, which incumbents are motivated and able to beat, from disruptive ones, which they ignore. He read the iPhone as the first kind. The prediction follows correctly from the model; the model was pointed at the wrong thing.
detailsBody: Christensen (1952–2020) was the Kim B. Clark Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School, and The Economist called him the most influential management thinker of his time — both per Wikipedia ↗.

A note on what this page does not do. The honest answer to “where exactly did he say it?” is that we could not open a primary source: Wikiquote’s citation has gone dead and the archive copy was unreachable from here. We would rather say that than print an interview date we never checked.
context.pull: The prediction was not a guess. It was the theory, applied — which is why the miss mattered.
